quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud and tap the beats as you go.
quests.hint: 'every', 'family' and 'interesting' are spelled with more syllables than they are said with: EV-ree, FAM-lee, IN-tres-ting.
quests.explanation: Count beats, not letters. Speakers often skip a weak middle vowel, so 'every' has two beats, 'family' two or three, and 'interesting' three.
quests.textToSpeak: Every evening, my family watches something interesting.

quests.instruction: Say it slowly, leaning on the stressed syllable of each long word (syllable counting: 3 and 4 beats).
quests.hint: Count the beats: 'library' (LI-brer-y, 3), 'collection' (col-LEC-tion, 3), 'geography' (ge-OG-ra-phy, 4).
quests.explanation: Each syllable holds one vowel beat. Strong syllables are longer and louder, weak ones are short. Don't drop the strong ones.
quests.textToSpeak: The library has a large collection of books about geography.
commonMistakes: Dropping the second syllable of 'library', as 'lie-ry'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a travel enquiry.
quests.hint: 'accommodation' has five syllables and 'transportation' has four. Each is stressed on the syllable just before -tion.
quests.explanation: The long -tion words share a pattern: stress falls on the syllable right before -tion. Count the beats up to the stressed one and lean on it.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you send some details about the accommodation and the transportation?

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress on the first syllable).
quests.hint: 'weather', 'lovely', 'picnic' and 'garden' all put stress on the first syllable: WEA-ther, LOVE-ly, PIC-nic, GAR-den.
quests.explanation: Most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are stressed on the first syllable. Make it longer, louder and higher, and keep the second syllable weak.
quests.textToSpeak: The weather was lovely, so we had a picnic in the garden.
commonMistakes: Saying the weak vowel in '-den' as a full [e]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a report of a theft.
quests.hint: 'police', 'guitar' and 'hotel' break the pattern: the stress is on the second syllable: po-LICE, gui-TAR, ho-TEL.
quests.explanation: A few common nouns carry stress on the second syllable, often words that came from other languages. Learn them as exceptions, with a weak first syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: The police found my guitar outside the hotel.
commonMistakes: Saying 'police' as 'pol-ice' with a full first vowel
Giving 'guitar' equal stress on both syllables

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a complaint.
quests.hint: 'machine' is ma-CHINE, but 'station' and 'ticket' are STA-tion and TIC-ket.
quests.explanation: Notice how the stress moves: weak-strong in 'machine', strong-weak in 'station' and 'ticket'. The stressed syllable gets the clearest vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: The machine at the station swallowed my ticket.
commonMistakes: Saying 'MAchine' with stress on the first syllable
Saying 'staTION' with stress on the second
Making the vowel in 'ma-' a full [æ]

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (verb stress on the second syllable).
quests.hint: 'explain' and 'accept' have stress on the second syllable: ex-PLAIN, ac-CEPT. 'decided' is de-CI-ded.
quests.explanation: Most two-syllable verbs stress the second syllable, with a short, weak first syllable. Don't let the first vowel become a full vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: Can you explain why you decided to accept the offer?
quests.targetPhoneme: verb stress on the second syllable
commonMistakes: Saying the first vowel of 'accept' as a full [æ]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as an apology for a late arrival.
quests.hint: 'delayed', 'arrived', 'forgot' and 'inform' all carry stress on the second syllable.
quests.explanation: Each verb has a weak first syllable that leads into the strong second one. Say them with a small rise into the stressed vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: The flight was delayed, so we arrived late and I forgot to inform you.
quests.targetPhoneme: verb stress on the second syllable

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a work plan.
quests.hint: 'answer' and 'visit' are exceptions with stress on the first syllable; 'prepare' follows the verb pattern.
quests.explanation: Some common verbs stress the first syllable, usually those ending in a weak syllable such as -er, -it or -en. Learn the frequent ones as a group.
quests.textToSpeak: Let me answer the phone, then I'll visit the site and prepare a summary.
commonMistakes: Stressing the second syllable of 'answer' or 'visit'
Saying 'summary' with stress on the second syllable

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (noun/verb stress: record).
quests.hint: The noun is REcord (stress first) and the verb is reCORD (stress second).
quests.explanation: In many two-syllable pairs, the noun stresses the first syllable and the verb stresses the second. The vowels change too: the unstressed syllable becomes weak.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you record the call? I want a record of what they promised.
quests.phoneticHint: The noun is [ˈrekərd] and the verb is [rɪˈkɔːrd].
commonMistakes: Using the same stress for both words
Stressing the first syllable of the verb
Keeping a full vowel in the unstressed first syllable of the verb

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a complaint about rising costs.
quests.hint: The verb is inCREASE; the noun is INcrease.
quests.explanation: Stress the second syllable of the verb and the first syllable of the noun. Make the stressed syllable higher and clearer; the other is short.
quests.textToSpeak: They increase the rent every year, and this year the increase is huge.
quests.phoneticHint: The verb is [ɪnˈkriːs] and the noun is [ˈɪnkriːs].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as an official notice.
quests.hint: The noun is PERmit; the verb is perMIT.
quests.explanation: The vowels tell you which word it is: a strong [ɜː] in the noun's first syllable and a weak [ə] in the verb's first syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: You need a permit, and the council won't permit parking here.
quests.phoneticHint: The noun is [ˈpɜːrmɪt] and the verb is [pərˈmɪt].
commonMistakes: Saying the verb with the noun's stress: 'PERmit'
Pronouncing the first vowel of the verb as [ɜː]

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (three-syllable stress patterns).
quests.hint: 'engineer' is en-gi-NEER (stress last), 'Monday' is MON-day, and 'holiday' is HOL-i-day (stress first).
quests.explanation: Three-syllable words can be stressed on the first, second or third syllable. Words ending in -eer carry final stress; many others stress the first syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll call the engineer on Monday, before the holiday.
commonMistakes: Making the last syllable of 'holiday' as strong as the first

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a shopping list.
quests.hint: Stress the middle syllable in all three: ba-NA-na, po-TA-to, to-MA-to.
quests.explanation: The first syllable is weak (a schwa), the middle is strong and long, and the last is weak again. Aim for a quick–long–quick rhythm.
quests.textToSpeak: We need a banana, a potato and a tomato.
quests.phoneticHint: 'banana' is [bəˈnænə], 'potato' is [pəˈteɪtoʊ], and 'tomato' is [təˈmeɪtoʊ] in American English.
commonMistakes: Saying the first vowel as a full [æ]
Giving equal weight to all three syllables

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a receptionist.
quests.hint: 'assistant' is a-SIS-tant, 'available' is a-VAIL-a-ble, and 'tomorrow' is to-MOR-row.
quests.explanation: In all three, the first syllable is weak and the second is stressed. The syllables after the stress get short and quiet.
quests.textToSpeak: The assistant said the manager isn't available until tomorrow.
quests.targetPhoneme: stress on the second syllable of longer words
commonMistakes: Saying 'assistant' with stress on the last syllable
Saying the first vowel of 'tomorrow' as a full [oʊ]

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress before -tion and -sion).
quests.hint: 'decision', 'promotion' and 'presentation' all put main stress on the syllable before the ending: de-CI-sion, pro-MO-tion, pre-sen-TA-tion.
quests.explanation: Words ending in -tion and -sion stress the syllable right before the ending. The ending itself is weak [ʃən].
quests.textToSpeak: The decision about the promotion depends on the presentation.
commonMistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'tee-on' instead of a weak [ʃən]

quests.instruction: Say it slowly, leaning on the stressed syllable of each long word (stress before -tion).
quests.hint: 'communication' stresses CA, 'conversation' stresses SA, and 'successful' stresses CESS.
quests.explanation: In long -tion words, the stress is on the syllable before -tion and the earlier syllables are weak. Say the stressed beat clearly and let the rest flow.
quests.textToSpeak: Good communication is the key to a successful conversation.
commonMistakes: Saying 'successful' with stress on the first syllable

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a complaint about an online form.
quests.hint: 'application' is ap-pli-CA-tion and 'confirmation' is con-fir-MA-tion.
quests.explanation: The stressed syllable is [eɪ] before -tion in both words. Lengthen and raise it; the earlier syllables stay short.
quests.textToSpeak: I completed the application, but I never got a confirmation.

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress before -ic).
quests.hint: 'electric', 'fantastic' and 'realistic' all stress the syllable before -ic: e-LEC-tric, fan-TAS-tic, re-a-LIS-tic.
quests.explanation: Words ending in -ic stress the syllable immediately before the ending. Lean on that syllable; the -ic itself is short.
quests.textToSpeak: The electric car looks fantastic, but it isn't very realistic for a big family.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a positive assessment.
quests.hint: 'logical' (LOG-i-cal), 'practical' (PRAC-ti-cal) and 'economical' (e-co-NOM-i-cal) stress the syllable before -ical.
quests.explanation: -ical follows the same rule as -ic: the syllable before the ending takes stress. In 'economical', that is the third syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: That's a logical, practical and economical solution.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a medical update.
quests.hint: 'physical' and 'chemical' stress the first syllable, while 'analysis' stresses the second: a-NAL-y-sis.
quests.explanation: 'physical' and 'chemical' stress the syllable before -ical. 'analysis' follows a different pattern: stress on the second syllable and two weak syllables after.
quests.textToSpeak: The physical check-up and the chemical analysis were normal.

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress before -ity).
quests.hint: 'possibility' (pos-si-BIL-i-ty) and 'electricity' (e-lec-TRIC-i-ty) stress the syllable before -ity.
quests.explanation: Words ending in -ity stress the syllable right before the ending. The ending is weak and quick. Because the words are long, only one syllable stands out.
quests.textToSpeak: There's a possibility that the electricity will go off.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a request at work.
quests.hint: 'clarify' (CLAR-i-fy) and 'simplify' (SIM-pli-fy) put the stress on the first syllable; the -ify is weak.
quests.explanation: In these verbs, stress falls two syllables before the end. The final -fy keeps its [aɪ] glide, but it is lighter than the stressed vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you clarify the plan and simplify the process?

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a short bio.
quests.hint: 'photography' is pho-TOG-ra-phy and 'biography' is bi-OG-ra-phy: stress on the syllable before -graphy.
quests.explanation: The stress lands on the syllable before -graphy. The first syllable is weak. Compare 'photograph', which stresses the first syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: She studied photography at college, then wrote a biography of her teacher.
commonMistakes: Saying 'photography' with the same stress as 'photograph'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would give directions Watch the stress in compound nouns.
quests.hint: In each compound the first word is stressed: BUS stop, POST office, CAR park.
quests.explanation: Compound nouns put the main stress on the first part. The second part is weaker, lower in pitch and shorter.
quests.textToSpeak: The bus stop is next to the post office and the car park.
quests.phoneticHint: 'bus stop' is [ˈbʌs stɒp], 'post office' is [ˈpoʊst ɒfɪs], and 'car park' is [ˈkɑːr pɑːrk].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a shopping list Watch the compound stress vs single-word stress.
quests.hint: 'toothbrush' and 'toothpaste' stress the first part; 'shampoo' stresses the last syllable.
quests.explanation: Two-part compounds like 'toothbrush' stress the first part. 'shampoo' isn't a compound and follows a different rule: sham-POO.
quests.textToSpeak: Get a new toothbrush and a tube of toothpaste, plus a bottle of shampoo.
commonMistakes: Saying 'toothpaste' with equal stress on both parts

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a correction.
quests.hint: The stress moves to the word that changes: BUS station, not TRAIN station.
quests.explanation: When you correct information, put the main stress on the word that carries the contrast, even inside a compound.
quests.textToSpeak: Meet me at the bus station, not the train station.
quests.phoneticHint: 'bus station' is [ˈbʌs ˈsteɪʃən] and 'train station' is [ˈtreɪn ˈsteɪʃən] with the contrast on the first word.
commonMistakes: Giving no extra stress to 'bus' and 'train'

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress in longer everyday words).
quests.hint: 'temperature' (TEM-pra-chur), 'uncomfortable' (un-COM-fort-a-ble) and 'adjust' (ad-JUST) each have one clear stress.
quests.explanation: Long words keep one main stress; the rest go weak. 'temperature' loses a syllable in speech, and 'uncomfortable' can be said with four beats.
quests.textToSpeak: The temperature in the room is uncomfortable, so could you adjust it?
commonMistakes: Saying 'temperature' with four equal beats, as 'tem-per-a-ture'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a workplace suggestion.
quests.hint: 'opportunity' stresses TU, 'improve' stresses PROVE, 'communication' stresses CA, and 'departments' stresses PART.
quests.explanation: Four different words, four different stress spots. Find the stressed beat first, then say the others quietly around it.
quests.textToSpeak: There's an opportunity to improve communication between our departments.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as an event announcement.
quests.hint: 'international' (in-ter-NA-tion-al), 'conference' (CON-fer-ence) and 'sustainability' (sus-tain-a-BIL-i-ty).
quests.explanation: Long words often have a main stress and a lighter secondary stress earlier. Give the main stress to the marked syllable, and a lighter one earlier in the word.
quests.textToSpeak: The international conference on sustainability is completely full.
commonMistakes: Dropping the last two syllables of 'sustainability'
